A1.justification: Despite retitling, both PDFs describe the same Pythia robustness study using GCG, RandomToken and adversarial training. Their text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 Sections 4–5 and Appendices D–E report original classification accuracy, attack success, adversarial training and robustness-transfer results.

after.justification: v3 Sections 4–6 and the appendices report original robustness experiments, attack and defense compute analyses, and transfer evaluations.

M1.justification: v1 repeatedly trains on a growing dataset augmented with adversarial examples. v3 replaces this with fixed-size training samples drawn from clean data and an adversarial pool, prioritizes adversarial examples by loss and recency, and progressively increases attack strength (Appendix D). These change the training procedure, while the Pythia classification architecture and basic attack algorithms remain.

E1.justification: v3 expands fine-tuned evaluation from four tasks to six by adding Helpful and Harmless preference classification. It also introduces attacks inserted 90% into the variable prompt text. Conversely, stronger-attack and cross-attack transfer results previously shown for all four original tasks are now reported only for Spam and IMDB.

E2.justification: The fine-tuned comparisons retain both GCG and RandomToken. However, v1 also evaluates RandomToken-trained models against RandomToken itself (Figures 17–20); v3 omits that comparison arm while retaining RandomToken training in the GCG-transfer evaluation. No new independent baseline family is introduced.

E3.justification: Fine-tuning changes from one to three epochs and from whole filtered datasets to 20,000-example subsets, with the length cutoff reduced from 2,000 to 1,000 tokens. Adversarial training extends beyond 909M to 2.6B parameters, uses size-dependent training budgets, and reports 500 validation examples instead of 200. Transfer evaluation changes from 30-iteration to 128-iteration GCG, alongside revised training attack strengths.

E4.justification: v3 adds systematic attack-compute sensitivity analyses, regression-slope comparisons before and after adversarial training, offense–defense analysis at a 5% target attack success rate, and suffix-to-infix robustness testing. v1's investigation of pretraining-checkpoint and classification-head initialization variability is no longer reported. The new infix test directly examines whether defenses merely learn to ignore suffixes.

E5.justification: Fine-tuning figures report five random seeds in v3 versus three in v1; adversarial-training figures retain three-seed median and min–max reporting. v3 also introduces regression fits with R-squared reporting and interpolation of compute at target attack success rates. These extend statistical estimation without introducing confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Results are substantially replaced and expanded. v1 Figure 3b shows strong RandomToken-to-GCG transfer for larger models, whereas v3 Figure 22 supports only limited transfer under its stronger evaluation; this is not a same-setting performance decline. v3 adds compute-scaling, offense–defense and infix-transfer results, while removing v1's per-model clean-validation accuracy table.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix C.2.1 adds a conditional derivation connecting a linear relationship between logit attack success and log compute to logistic success probabilities and limiting power laws for success and failure. v1 has no corresponding mathematical argument. This is a limited analytical addition rather than a new theoretical framework.

C1.justification: v3 adds central claims that adversarial training improves robustness much more compute-efficiently than model scaling and that offense–defense scaling favors offense or reaches approximate parity, depending on the setting. Its abstract also describes undefended scaling benefits as modest and task-dependent, replacing v1's 'little to no benefit' summary. The contribution shifts toward quantified attack and defense scaling.

C2.justification: v1 interprets cross-attack transfer optimistically as potentially emerging with scale. v3 qualifies this interpretation after finding limited RandomToken-to-GCG transfer and explicitly leaves attack weakness versus attack type unresolved. It adds interpretations of infix transfer and offense–defense slopes, plus substantive limitations concerning classification-to-generation generalization and relative versus absolute attack costs.

D1.justification: v3 supplies replay-sampling equations and weights, attack schedules, expanded prompt examples, FLOP accounting, interpolation pseudocode and disclosure of a multi-GPU FLOP-estimation correction. Earlier explicit dataset URLs and the detailed model-size table disappear. Documentation is substantially expanded, although Appendix D's fixed per-round training size conflicts with Appendix E.2's description of increasing examples per round.

R1.justification: v3 adds discussion of Yang et al. (2024), contrasting its substitution attacks and label ambiguity with this study, and adds citations supporting preference data and offense–defense framing. The introduction newly claims the first publicly available large-scale investigation. Most of the existing related-work discussion remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, experimental narrative, transfer discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Existing material is reorganized around model-size, attack-compute and defense-compute questions, with fine-tuning setup moved into methodology and substantially revised appendix organization. The title and author information also change.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main text to a predominantly single-column layout, consolidates task plots, introduces extensive logit/log-compute displays, redraws the training diagram and expands examples into tables highlighting attack tokens. Several earlier tables and displays disappear. Figure 4 incorrectly duplicates the Spam panel despite promising IMDB; the distinct IMDB panel appears in Figure 18.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v1's largely training-round-based scaling evidence through direct attack/defense-compute comparisons and suffix-to-infix testing, addressing important budget-comparability and shortcut-learning questions. Stronger transfer evaluations also motivate more restrained interpretations. These gains outweigh material presentation and reproducibility drawbacks, especially the duplicated Figure 4 panel, broken references and conflicting per-round training-size descriptions in Appendices D and E.2.
